**A code model needs a task definition before a training recipe.** Completing the next line, repairing a repository bug, writing tests, and explaining code require different context and evaluation. Decide which behavior matters, in which languages and environments, before collecting examples or selecting an adaptation method.

**An end-to-end example.** For repository bug fixing, each training example should contain the relevant repository snapshot, issue description, permitted tools, and a verified repair. The evaluation must run meaningful hidden tests or check final repository behavior. Merely reproducing the patch text is too narrow: several correct fixes can differ syntactically, while a familiar-looking patch can still be wrong.

**Why split before generating examples.** If two nearly identical repositories appear on both sides of the split, evaluation can measure memorization. Repository/time separation and duplicate detection should happen before deriving many files or issue variants from the same source. Otherwise one original project can leak through hundreds of superficially different examples.

Start with a pretrained baseline and compare supervised adaptation, parameter-efficient tuning, or preference optimization only when the data supports them. A preference pair should encode a meaningful improvement such as passing tests or avoiding an API misuse, not an arbitrary stylistic preference. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)

**Count success honestly.** Report first-attempt correctness and success under a stated sample/tool budget. Generating 100 candidates and selecting the one passing visible tests is a different product from producing one reliable answer. Include latency, compute, security of execution, and regressions on supported tasks when deciding whether adaptation was worthwhile.

**Technical details and references.**

Define the target languages, repository tasks, execution environment, and acceptable latency before choosing training. Build a consented, license-reviewed repository corpus with dependency manifests and snapshots. Split by repository and time before generating examples; remove near duplicates and benchmark contamination across training and evaluation. Examples should include realistic repository context and executable task specifications.

Begin with SFT on high-quality demonstrations. Generate additional candidates in isolated execution sandboxes with no secrets/network, bounded CPU/memory/time, and read-only base images. Compile, lint, and run hidden tests; passing visible tests alone does not prove correctness. Save tests, environment hashes, and execution traces with each accepted example.

Use preference optimization or execution-reward RL only if the reward predicts held-out usefulness. Counter reward hacking with fresh/private tests and penalize undesirable side effects. Mix general code tasks, retain a reference/KL constraint where appropriate, and monitor broad capability suites to detect forgetting. Compare adapter tuning with full tuning on quality and serving cost. Release a versioned checkpoint through shadow and canary stages; retain the old model and dataset lineage for rollback.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** For n sampled solutions with c passing tests, the usual estimator is $pass@k=1-\binom{n-c}{k}/\binom nk$ when the sampling conditions apply. It measures success under a sampling budget, not universal coding ability. Include repository-level contamination checks and hidden behavioral tests, since memorized examples or shallow tests can inflate the apparent gain. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://huggingface.co/blog/pref-tuning) and [2](https://huggingface.co/blog/the-stack).
